extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) responding to PTO rejections
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using MPEP Chapter 2100 (sections 2105-2186) to rebut or defend against PTO rejections under 35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, and 112; includes which MPEP headings summarize judicial rules, how to cite them, and when to rely on case law instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Chapter 2100 to rebut examiner rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 2100 incorporates judicial doctrines and case summaries relevant to §§ 101, 102, 103 and 112 and may be cited to rebut prima facie findings of anticipation or obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite MPEP sections that articulate the judicial rule and (when present) include the case summary in Chapter 2100 so the examiner can quickly verify the rule; prefer citing MPEP where it accurately captures case facts because examiners are trained on and charged to follow the MPEP and it is readily available in their offices. Beware that some MPEP sections may be incomplete or outdated relative to Federal Circuit precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility doctrines under §101
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP §2107 and related subsections present doctrines such as 'real world value,' 'wholly inoperative inventions,' 'incredible utility,' 'therapeutic or pharmacological utility,' and state that 'an asserted utility creates a presumption of utility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use §2107 for general utility rejections; cite summarized cases in Chapter 2100 (for example In re Jolles and Cross v. Iizuka) to clarify therapeutic/pharmacological utility. For field-specific utility issues, consult §2105 (living organisms) and §2106 headings I–IV (computer programs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requirement (102) — teach every element
rubrics_metrics.description: TO ANTICIPATE A CLAIM, THE REFERENCE MUST TEACH EVERY ELEMENT OF THE CLAIM (MPEP §2131 heading).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite §2131 when a reference does not disclose all claim elements to rebut anticipation. Use subsections dealing with multiple-reference anticipation and genus/species situations where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and subparts of §102 (2132-2138)
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP §§2132-2138 define sub-parts of 35 U.S.C. §102(a)-(g) and key terms such as 'known or used', 'in this country', 'on sale', and 'public use'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these subsections to challenge applicability of a cited reference by attacking whether the statutory elements for the particular §102 subsection are met (e.g., territoriality, on-sale/public-use bars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for prima facie 102(a) and applicant's own-work exception (2132.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection 2132.01 provides the test for establishing a prima facie rejection under 35 U.S.C. §102(a) and guidelines for establishing an exception showing the reference's disclosure was the applicant's own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an examiner relies on §102(a), use 2132.01 to demand the showing required for a prima facie case and to present evidence that the reference was applicant's own work (and thus not proper prior art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception to public use bar (2133.03(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection 2133.03(e) provides guidelines for applying an experimental use exception to the public use bar under 35 U.S.C. §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the alleged public use was experimental, cite this subsection and the tests/summaries it provides to show the activity was not a statutory public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors for obviousness (2141 / Graham v. John Deere)
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP §2141 lists the four factual inquiries from Graham v. John Deere: (1) scope and content of prior art; (2) differences between prior art and claims at issue; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) secondary considerations (objective indicia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame responses to obviousness rejections by addressing all four Graham inquiries and use §2141 as the canonical statement of that framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic considerations for obviousness (MPEP §2143)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2143 prescribes basic considerations: (1) consider the claimed invention as a whole; (2) consider the references as a whole and require that they suggest desirability of combining; (3) disallow impermissible hindsight; (4) use a standard of reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on these tenets to challenge improper obviousness findings (e.g., failure to consider all claim limitations or use of hindsight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part test for combining references (2143 subsections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2143 divides the criteria that must be met to combine references into (1) some suggestion or motivation (from references or general knowledge) to modify or combine; (2) reasonable expectation of success; (3) the references (alone or combined) must teach or suggest all claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use §2143 and its subsections (including 2143.01, 2143.02, 2143.03) to require the examiner to show each part of this test when asserting a combination rejection; cite specific case summaries included in Chapter 2100 (e.g., In re Gordon) when analogies apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification cannot render prior art unsatisfactory (Gordon rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: One judicial rule listed in Subsection 2143.01 is that 'THE PROPOSED MODIFICATION CANNOT RENDER THE PRIOR ART UNSATISFACTORY FOR ITS INTENDED PURPOSE' (summary of In re Gordon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner's proposed modification would make the prior art inoperable or unsatisfactory for its intended purpose, cite 2143.01 and the Gordon summary (example: flipping an oil/water filter to make an air/blood filter would render it inoperable). Use analogies to the examiner's combination to show the modification is not a legitimate motivation to combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of material for obviousness; reliance on common knowledge (2144 & 2144.03)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2144 lists sources an examiner may use for an obviousness rejection; Subsection 2144.03 provides guidance for relying upon common knowledge or 'well known' prior art and requires the examiner, upon challenge, to cite a reference to support such reliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an examiner's combination relies on 'common knowledge' rather than a specific citation, require citation per 2144.03. Use §2144 to question whether the asserted sources legitimately supply the missing teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness for claims with ranges (2144.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection 2144.05 provides guidance as to when to apply an obviousness rejection to a claim reciting a range of components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite 2144.05 to challenge improper extrapolation from a prior-art value to a claimed range or to demand a showing that the range itself would have been obvious to try with a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness of species when prior art teaches genus; close structural similarity (2144.08, 2144.09)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsections 2144.08 and 2144.09 address obviousness of species when prior art teaches a genus and when a reference has close structural similarity to the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these subsections in chemical and composition cases to argue against blanket genus-to-species obviousness or to require the examiner to show specific motivation to narrow/modify the genus to the claimed species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments to avoid or use (2145 headings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2145 includes several arguments practitioners should avoid (e.g., arguing the age of a reference), but also lists valid arguments such as that a prior art reference 'teaches away' from the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on weak/forbidden arguments listed in 2145(h); instead cite MPEP-discussed persuasive arguments (e.g., teaching away) supported by case summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation rules (2111-2116) — preambles and transitional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 2111-2116 govern interpretation of various claim types; Subsection 2111.02 describes interpretation of claim preambles and 2111.03 discusses transitional phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these sections to argue correct claim scope and that the examiner misinterpreted claim language (e.g., improper treatment of preamble or transitional language).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art disclosure threshold, operability, and enabling prior art (2121-2129, 2121.01, 2121.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 2121-2129 discuss what is required for a reference to constitute prior art, including disclosure threshold for operability (2121.01) and what compounds/compositions constitute enabling prior art (2121.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge a reference's applicability by attacking disclosure threshold, operability, or enabling status using the cited subsections and their case summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date foreign patent as prior art (2126.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection 2126.01 instructs that the date a foreign patent becomes available as a reference is usually the date of patent enforceability, while noting exceptions (e.g., countries maintaining patent secrecy; possible exceptions such as publication prior to issuance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite 2126.01 when disputing the effective date of a foreign patent as prior art and check for listed exceptions and additional authorities (MPEP §901.05, Chisum) referenced by the MPEP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publications as prior art — public accessibility and date (2128)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2128 provides guidelines for using printed publications as prior art, including establishing the required level of public accessibility and the date the publication was available as a reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 2128 to attack an examiner's assertion that a document is a printed publication (demand proof of public accessibility and correct date) or to show a publication is not properly a prior-art printed publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: §112 first paragraph: written description, enablement, best mode (2163-2165)
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP divides the first paragraph requirement into written description (Section 2163), enablement (2164), and best mode (2165). Subsection 2106.01 discusses these requirements for computer programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with §112 first-paragraph rejections, address the separate tests and cite the appropriate MPEP subsection; for software, use 2106.01 for special considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: §112 second paragraph — definiteness and claiming requirements (2171, 2173)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2171 lays out the second-paragraph requirements: (1) claims must set forth the subject matter applicants regard as their invention; (2) claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the subject matter. Subsection 2173.04 restates that 'breadth of a claim is not to be equated with indefiniteness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these sections to respond to indefiniteness or breadth rejections; cite subsections on claim terminology, negative limitations, aggregation, and prolix where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: §112 sixth paragraph — means-plus-function treatment and equivalence (2181-2184)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 2181-2186 provide guidance for claims under the sixth paragraph: an element expressed as a means/step for performing a specified function shall be construed to cover corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents; Section 2183 explains the examiner's prima facie case of equivalence and the resulting burden shift to the applicant; Section 2184 guides the examiner in determining whether applicant has met the burden of proving nonequivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To rebut means-plus-function equivalence findings, use the list of acceptable nonequivalence arguments: (1) specification teachings that particular prior art is not equivalent; (2) teachings in the prior art that show nonequivalence; (3) Rule 132 affidavit evidence. Cite 2183–2184 to require the examiner to make a proper prima facie showing and to define applicant's burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP vs Federal Circuit conflicts — verify and supplement with case law
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Chapter 2100 sections incorporate only part of case law or outdated rules; the PTO has sometimes failed to follow Federal Circuit precedent (examples: Donaldson, Danley, Twin Discs/Self).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely blindly on MPEP; verify the cited rule against controlling Federal Circuit precedent and cite case law where Chapter 2100 is incomplete or conflicts with the Federal Circuit. When MPEP adopts an overly broad or outdated rule (e.g., teaching away not pertinent to anticipation in §2131.05), use controlling cases such as In re Marosi to counter the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of functional limitations (functional language and apparatus claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 2100 includes guidance that functional limitations should often be treated as 'means-plus-function' under §112 (sixth paragraph), and cites sections to use when a functional limitation is rejected under anticipation or obviousness (e.g., §2131, §2143.03, §2173.05(g), §2181). The MPEP contains conflicting guidance (e.g., Danley vs later cases like Swinehart) but ultimately treats functional limitations via §112 principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with a functional-language rejection, cite §2131 or §2143.03 depending on anticipation vs obviousness, then §2173.05(g) for support that functional claim elements are permissible, and §2181 to demand means-plus-function treatment; if MPEP is inconsistent, supplement with Federal Circuit case law (Swinehart, Donaldson, etc.).
